name: Marcus Aurelius
summary: Marcus Aurelius was a Stoic who held that all rational people share one reason and one common good, and who wrote that virtue matters more than wealth, fame or pleasure. As emperor he fought the Marcomannic and Parthian wars, ruled through the Senate and the courts, and passed power to his son Commodus. Most of what is known of his political acts comes from later ancient historians, and his own words survive mainly in the Meditations.

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.usedFor: summary of the record: legal reforms on manumission and guardianship, appointments, Christian persecution and its disputed imperial role, succession to Commodus, currency debasement

state-harmful.rationale: He served as emperor and treats membership of a commonwealth as natural to a rational creature (Meditations IV, VI), so the state is for him a necessary part of human life.

more-religion-public.rationale: Dio calls him so godfearing that his piety showed even on the unlucky days (dies nefasti), and HA says he revived the worship of the gods and summoned priests before the Marcomannic war.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: HA records that he zealously revived the worship of the traditional gods, and his reign restored traditional public rites.

gradual-change.rationale: Inferred: he revived older religious worship and kept the Senate and magistracies in use (HA, Dio), which suggests respect for established institutions; he says nothing about the pace of change.

reduce-immigration.rationale: He banished the Germanic settlers from Italy after the Ravenna revolt, but he also settled tribes in the frontier provinces (Wikipedia), so the record points both ways.

nation-first.rationale: Meditations VI (section XXXIX): his city and country as Antoninus is Rome, but as a man it is the whole world, and what serves the wider common good is what is good for him.

open-borders.rationale: Wikipedia says he banished the Germanic settlers brought into Italy after a revolt at Ravenna, which runs against open borders.

revolution-justified.rationale: Dio records that Marcus had to put down Cassius's usurpation in Syria, which he treated as a threat to the state; he wrote no general view on revolution.

tax-inheritance.rationale: HA says he enacted laws about inheritance taxes, but the rates and direction of those laws are not recorded.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: he accepted the dynastic arrangement and passed power to his son, which implies that a hereditary line can rule, but he wrote nothing on monarchy as an institution.

war-builds-character.rationale: Dio quotes him: 'Such things accursed war brings in its train', which calls war an evil rather than a source of character.

separate-church-state.rationale: He was elected pontifex maximus, chief priest of the official Roman cults (Wikipedia), so the office of head of state was joined to the state religion.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Meditations VI (section XLIX): 'That which is not good for the bee-hive, cannot be good for the bee.' He ties the individual's good to the common good.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Inferred: his ethic is built on duties to the common good (Meditations II and VI), and he never speaks of rights, so the priority claim is only indirectly supported.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Meditations III (section II) finds beauty in the natural processes of ageing and ripening, but he does not discuss value apart from human use.

positive-liberty.rationale: Meditations treats external things such as wealth as indifferent, and freedom as an inner matter, which runs against the claim that freedom needs material means.

territorial-expansion.rationale: HA says he wished to make a province of Marcomannia and Sarmatia, and Wikipedia says the annexation was cut short by Cassius's revolt and his death.

universal-morality.rationale: Meditations IV: reason is common to all people, and the law that reason prescribes is common too, so all are fellow-citizens of one commonwealth.

single-common-good.rationale: Meditations VI (section XLIX) and VII treat the good of the whole, the hive, as the only standard, which favours one common good, though he does not discuss competing group interests.

rule-by-example.rationale: HA says he restrained men from evil and urged them to good by reason, rather than relying on punishment alone.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He makes reason the guide to conduct in the Meditations, but he also prays to the gods and accepts providence, so the evidence points both ways.

class-collaboration.rationale: Inferred: Meditations I (section XV) holds that people are born to cooperate rather than oppose one another, but it speaks of humanity in general, not of employers and workers.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Meditations I (section XI) lists as an ideal an equal commonwealth administered by justice and equality; he also held that all share one reason. He kept slavery in place, so the support is partial.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Meditations XI (section XVI) says people are not born to hurt one, and that is against nature, but he fought wars, so this is mixed with his own record.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Meditations I (section XV) says opposition between people is against nature and that people are born to cooperate; progress is not discussed.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He commanded the armies in person against the Marcomanni and Quadi and in the eastern war (Dio, epitome of Book 72), and he replaced the empire's major officials and appointed prefects (Wikipedia).

death-penalty.rationale: HA says he held trials that involved the death penalty and was implacable toward those clearly guilty of serious crimes, but he is also reported to have punished crimes more lightly than the law allowed.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Meditations I (section XI) sets out an ideal of an equal commonwealth with equal laws, and HA says he added court days until 230 were set for pleading cases; he is not presented as above the law.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: HA says he gave the insignia of office and privileges to all his kin, and to Verus's sisters and kin after Verus's death.

elective-rulers.rationale: He accepted the adoptive succession arranged by Hadrian and Antoninus, and in the end passed power to his son rather than to an elected successor.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Dio says that most of his life was devoted to beneficence, but gives no account of help to the poor.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Meditations IV recommends retiring into oneself, but he also insists on doing public duty (Meditations VI), and he governed the empire in person through its wars.

native-born-offices.rationale: He gave command to Albinus, a man of African origin (Marcus's letter in Fronto's correspondence), and appointed Titus Varius Clemens, from Pannonia, to head the imperial correspondence (Wikipedia).

filial-duty.rationale: Meditations I opens with thanks to his grandfather and mother, and Book VI speaks of honouring one's own mother; the duty of care is not stated outright.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Meditations I (section I) says to avoid the excess that comes with great wealth, and Meditations III and XIII treat riches and pleasure as not worth pursuing.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Dio says he neither slew nor imprisoned the senators who had been associated with Cassius, and HA says he suffered rather than ordered the execution of Cassius.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Wikipedia says persecution of Christians appears to have increased during his reign, but his personal role is unclear and much debated; his Meditations (XI, section III) mentions Christians only to criticise them.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Dio says he did not collect money from the subject nations and refused to raise new taxes, which runs against exploiting colonies for the ruling country's benefit.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred: Meditations X (section VIII) endorses leaving life by a plain voluntary act when one cannot act well, but it does not address medical help.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Dio reports him telling the troops that the fate of the sovereignty lay with Heaven alone; this is a secondhand report of his words.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He made his son Commodus Caesar in 166, took him as co-emperor in 177, and commended him to the army as his successor at his death (Dio, epitome of Book 72; Wikipedia). Late reports say he doubted Commodus (HA), which does not change the choice he made.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: HA says he added court-days so that cases were pleaded and judged, and appointed a special praetor for wards; emperors also issued rescripts case by case, so the record is mixed.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Meditations XI (section III) criticises the readiness of Christians to die as mere opposition and calls for death to be a matter of judgment, without stage-heroics.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Meditations I (section XV) describes each person as sharing a divine particle of reason, which he treats as a higher part of human nature; the political side is not discussed.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: His wars were largely defensive (Dio), but he planned to annex Marcomannia and Sarmatia (HA, Wikipedia), so he did not restrict force to defence alone.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Meditations I (section XV): people are born to be fellow-workers like the feet, hands and eyelids, and each shares the same reason and divine particle; he treats this shared nature as the basis of mutual duty.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: HA says he punished crimes with lighter penalties than the laws usually imposed, which leaves sentencing to judicial discretion.

simple-living.rationale: Meditations I and XIII prize plainness and a limited life, and Wikipedia says he slept on the ground and dressed in a plain Greek cloak in his youth.

notes: Known answers rest on the Meditations and on his letters and record as emperor, reported by Cassius Dio and the Historia Augusta. The Historia Augusta is unreliable and is low confidence where it is the only source. Reports conflict on whether he doubted Commodus (HA) and on his role in the persecution of Christians (disputed). The widow-related legal reform named in the research brief was not found in the sources opened here. Most modern-institution statements are null because the sources do not address their wording.
